questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AS Bonding Shape and Structure Applications
questions.question: Draw ammonia and water shapes with lone pairs
questions.subtopic: AS VSEPR, molecular dipoles, intermolecular forces and ionic/covalent structures
questions.prompt: Using electron-pair repulsion, draw and label the three-dimensional shapes of NH₃ and H₂O, including the bonding and lone pairs on each central atom. State each H–central atom–H angle and explain why the angles differ from ideal tetrahedral 109.5°. [7 marks]
markPoints: Shows NH₃ as trigonal pyramidal, not trigonal planar.
Identifies three bond pairs and ONE lone pair on NH₃ nitrogen.
States NH₃ H–N–H angle of about 107°.
Shows H₂O as bent (non-linear), not linear.
Identifies two bond pairs and TWO lone pairs on H₂O oxygen.
States H₂O H–O–H angle of about 104.5°.
Explains lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond repulsions and extra angle compression by the second lone pair.
questions.modelAnswer: Draw NH₃ with N central, three N–H bonds in a trigonal pyramid and one lone pair; H–N–H≈107°. Draw H₂O bent about O with two O–H bonds and two lone pairs; H–O–H≈104.5°. Four electron domains seek tetrahedral separation, but lone pairs repel bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other (lone–lone strongest), compressing bond angles. H₂O has two lone pairs and a smaller bond angle than NH₃. Drawing marks must be checked from the actual sketch.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AS Bonding Shape and Structure Applications
questions.question: Deduce unfamiliar central-atom shape with six electron pairs
questions.subtopic: AS VSEPR, molecular dipoles, intermolecular forces and ionic/covalent structures
questions.prompt: Xenon tetrafluoride, XeF₄, has four Xe–F bond pairs and two lone pairs around the central Xe atom. Sulfur hexafluoride, SF₆, has six bond pairs and no lone pairs around sulfur. Deduce the electron-domain arrangement around each central atom, give each molecular shape, and state the characteristic adjacent F–central atom–F angles. Explain where the lone pairs sit in XeF₄. [6 marks]
markPoints: Counts six total electron domains for both central atoms.
Identifies the electron-domain arrangement as octahedral.
For SF₆ gives octahedral molecular shape.
For SF₆ gives adjacent F–S–F angle 90° (and opposite 180° if noted).
For XeF₄ gives square-planar molecular shape and 90° between adjacent bonds.
Explains XeF₄ lone pairs occupy opposite octahedral positions to minimise repulsion.
questions.modelAnswer: Both XeF₄ and SF₆ have six electron domains, whose preferred arrangement is octahedral. SF₆ has no lone pairs, so its molecular shape is octahedral, with 90° adjacent bond angles. XeF₄ has four bond pairs and two lone pairs. The two lone pairs are opposite each other to minimise repulsion; the four Xe–F bonds lie in a plane forming a square, with 90° adjacent F–Xe–F angles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AS Bonding Shape and Structure Applications
questions.question: Compare permanent dipoles in BF3, CO2 and water
questions.subtopic: AS VSEPR, molecular dipoles, intermolecular forces and ionic/covalent structures
questions.prompt: The B–F, C=O and O–H bonds are polar. Explain why BF₃ and CO₂ do not have permanent molecular dipoles whereas H₂O does. Give the shapes of all three molecules, identify the δ− end of an O–H bond, and explain why a molecule with polar bonds may be non-polar overall. [7 marks]
markPoints: Identifies BF₃ as trigonal planar and symmetric.
States BF₃ bond dipoles cancel, giving no net dipole.
Identifies CO₂ as linear and symmetric.
States its C=O dipoles cancel, giving no net dipole.
Identifies H₂O as bent.
Places δ− on oxygen and δ+ on hydrogen in an O–H bond.
Explains the bent geometry prevents O–H dipoles cancelling, producing a permanent dipole despite BF₃ and CO₂ each having polar bonds.
questions.modelAnswer: BF₃ is trigonal planar, with three identical B–F bond dipoles at 120°, cancelling by symmetry. CO₂ is linear; its two equal, opposing C=O bond dipoles also cancel. H₂O has a bent structure, so its O–H dipoles do not cancel. Oxygen is δ−, hydrogen δ+, and the water molecule has a permanent dipole. Molecular polarity depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles, not just whether individual bonds are polar.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AS Bonding Shape and Structure Applications
questions.question: Explain structure and electrical conductivity
questions.subtopic: AS VSEPR, molecular dipoles, intermolecular forces and ionic/covalent structures
questions.prompt: Compare sodium chloride, solid iodine, diamond and graphite. For each, identify the type of solid structure and whether it is expected to conduct electricity at room temperature. Explain the charge-carrier reasoning, including why molten NaCl differs from solid NaCl. [8 marks]
markPoints: NaCl is an ionic lattice; solid NaCl does not conduct because ions cannot move.
Molten NaCl conducts because ions become mobile.
Iodine is a simple molecular lattice; solid I₂ does not conduct because it has no mobile charged particles.
Diamond is a giant covalent/macromolecular lattice.
Diamond does not conduct as it has no mobile electrons or ions under ordinary conditions.
Graphite is a giant covalent/macromolecular layered lattice.
Graphite conducts along layers because of delocalised electrons.
Explains strong covalent bonding within graphite layers but comparatively weak intermolecular/dispersion attractions between the layers, rather than describing ionic conduction.
questions.modelAnswer: Solid NaCl is ionic: charged ions are fixed in a lattice, so it does not conduct; molten NaCl conducts as ions move. Iodine is a simple molecular solid (I₂ molecules held together by dispersion forces) and has no mobile charged carriers. Diamond is a giant covalent lattice with electrons localised in bonds and does not conduct under ordinary conditions. Graphite is a giant covalent layered structure with delocalised electrons able to move along its layers; weak forces between layers also explain their ability to slide.

questions.question: Explain hydrogen bonding, boiling points and ice density
questions.subtopic: AS VSEPR, molecular dipoles, intermolecular forces and ionic/covalent structures
questions.prompt: Water and methane have similar small molecular sizes but very different boiling points. Explain why water has a much higher boiling point, identifying the dominant intermolecular force in each substance. Then explain why ice can have a lower density than liquid water. [6 marks]
markPoints: Water contains polar O–H bonds and lone pairs on O, enabling hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
Identifies methane as non-polar, with only London dispersion forces between its molecules.
Explains hydrogen bonds between water molecules are much stronger than the London forces between methane molecules.
More energy is required to separate water molecules, so water has the higher boiling point.
In ice, hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in a relatively open ordered network.
The open ice lattice has a greater volume for the same mass than liquid water, giving lower density.
questions.modelAnswer: Water molecules contain strongly polar O–H bonds, and oxygen has lone pairs, so water forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Non-polar CH₄ molecules are held together by weaker London dispersion forces. More energy is needed to overcome hydrogen bonds, giving water a much higher boiling point. In ice, hydrogen bonding creates an open ordered network with relatively large gaps; liquid water can pack more closely. For equal mass the ice occupies more volume, so its density is lower.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AS Bonding Shape and Structure Applications
questions.question: Ionic formulae and dative bonding in ammonium salts
questions.subtopic: AS VSEPR, molecular dipoles, intermolecular forces and ionic/covalent structures
questions.prompt: A student combines the ions Al³⁺, SO₄²⁻, Ca²⁺, NO₃⁻ and NH₄⁺. Write the correct formulae for aluminium sulfate, calcium nitrate and ammonium sulfate, showing one charge balance. Explain how a co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond can be formed when ammonia combines with a proton. [7 marks]
markPoints: Writes aluminium sulfate as Al₂(SO₄)₃.
Shows 2×(+3)+3×(−2)=0 or an equivalent correct aluminium sulfate charge balance.
Writes calcium nitrate as Ca(NO₃)₂.
Writes ammonium sulfate as (NH₄)₂SO₄.
States NH₃ has a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen.
States H⁺ has an empty electron-accepting orbital/no electron to share in an ordinary covalent bond.
Explains both electrons in the new N→H bond originate from nitrogen; NH₄⁺ is formed with four equivalent N–H bonds after formation.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium sulfate is Al₂(SO₄)₃ because 2 Al³⁺ balances 3 SO₄²⁻: total charge +6−6=0. Calcium nitrate is Ca(NO₃)₂; ammonium sulfate is (NH₄)₂SO₄. NH₃ has a lone pair on nitrogen and H⁺ accepts this pair. A co-ordinate N→H bond forms because nitrogen donates both bonding electrons. NH₄⁺ then has four equivalent N–H bonds.
